explanations.answer: One is rich and one is poor
explanations.explanation: Rich and poor, that's how Nathan sets it up. He's the prophet the LORD sent to David, and he opens with two men in one city and a gap between them you can see from space. No fancy words needed. Any baker hearing it already knows who to root for.

explanations.answer: One is old and one is young
explanations.explanation: Nathan never says a word about age. The only difference he gives is “…one rich and the other poor.” I know it's tempting to picture a grumpy old man and a young fellow, but the story sticks to money. Keep your eyes on the bank accounts, not the birthdays.

explanations.answer: One is a king and one is a servant
explanations.explanation: A king and a servant makes sense, since Nathan is talking to a king. But the story says “…one rich and the other poor.” Nobody in it is called a king, and the poor man isn't called a servant either. Just a rich man, a poor man and a whole lot of trouble coming.

The rich man has “…a great number of sheep and cattle…” That man needs a calculator just to count them. Keep that number in your pocket, baker, because it's about to matter. Lots of animals on one side, and only one little lamb on the other.
The rich man has “…a great number of sheep and cattle…” It's the poor man who has just the one animal. I get why those two could blur together at a glance. Rich means lots, poor means one.

Daughter. The lamb grew up with the poor man and his children, and the text says it was “…like a daughter to him.” Think about that for a second. I think this man loved that little lamb like a member of the family.
A servant works for you, and this lamb never punched a clock. The text says it was “…like a daughter to him.” A lamb that drinks from your cup is not on the payroll, friend. That's family.

Brother is close, since it's family language too. But the text says the lamb was “…like a daughter to him.” Family, yes, just a different seat at the table. I think the poor man's heart was all in on that little lamb.

The poor man's lamb. The rich man “…refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle…” and took the poor man's lamb instead to prepare for his guest. He had a whole herd to pick from and walked right past it. That's like owning a bakery full of cookies and swiping the one your neighbor was saving.

One of his own sheep is exactly what you'd expect, and it's exactly what he didn't do. The text says he “…refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle…” He held back from his own animals. Then he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for his guest.

explanations.answer: A calf from his own herd
explanations.explanation: A calf from his own herd would've been the easy move, and a calf is cattle. But the text says he “…refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle…” His herd stayed untouched. The poor man's lamb is what ended up prepared for the guest.

David says, “As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die!” That's an oath, and he swears it while he's burning with anger. I bet David has no idea how close that sentence is about to land.

David swears, “As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die!” The text says he “…burned with anger against the man…” That's a serious oath, made by the life of the LORD Himself. Nathan lets him finish.

Four. David says, “Because he has done this thing and has shown no pity, he must pay for the lamb four times over.” The man's lack of pity is the reason he gives. David's math is strict, and he has no idea whose bill he's writing.
Two sounds fair, but David goes bigger. He says the man “…must pay for the lamb four times over.” Four, not two. David isn't in a bargaining mood.
Seven sounds big, but that's not the number David uses. He says the man “…must pay for the lamb four times over.” Count along: one, two, three, four. That's already plenty for one little lamb.
“You are that man!” Nathan tells David. Four words, no wind up. David just announced the verdict, and Nathan turns it around on him. I bet that room went dead quiet.

explanations.answer: That man lives in your city
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a mystery with a search party, but Nathan skips all that. He says, “You are that man!” No address, no directions. The man David just sentenced is the one standing in front of Nathan.
Nobody needs to go looking. Nathan says, “You are that man!” The man David just sentenced is right there with Nathan. I think the search ended the second Nathan opened his mouth.

True, and listen to the generosity. After listing what He gave, the LORD says, “…and if that was not enough, I would have given you even more.” David already had a kingdom, and there was still more on the table. The LORD wasn't running low.
The LORD says the opposite: “…and if that was not enough, I would have given you even more.” So the offer of more was real. He wasn't running low on anything. I think that's the part that stings.

Ammonites. The LORD says, “You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites.” The Ammonites were the people Israel was fighting in that war (2 Samuel 11:1). Uriah the Hittite, the husband of Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:3), died in that fighting, and the LORD still says David is the one who slew him. I think this part is heavy.

The Philistines did fight Israel earlier in David's life (1 Samuel 17:1), but they aren't named here. The LORD says, “You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites.” The Ammonites were the people Israel was fighting in that war (2 Samuel 11:1). I think this part is heavy.

The Moabites are people from the country of Moab (Ruth 1:1), and they aren't named here. The LORD says, “You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites.” The Ammonites were the people Israel was fighting in that war (2 Samuel 11:1). This is a heavy verse.

explanations.answer: David despised Him and took Uriah's wife
explanations.explanation: The LORD gives the reason Himself: “…because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.” We don't have to guess at it. He names two things, despising Him and taking Uriah's wife. A reason that clear needs no help from me.

explanations.answer: David stayed home from the war
explanations.explanation: David did stay in Jerusalem while the army fought (2 Samuel 11:1), but the LORD doesn't give that as His reason. He says, “…because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.” When the LORD states the reason, I stick with His.

explanations.answer: David forgot to thank Him for the kingdom
explanations.explanation: Nothing in these verses says David forgot to say thanks. The LORD's reason is “…because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.” He does remind David of the kingdom He gave him, but that isn't the reason He gives here.

explanations.answer: In broad daylight before all Israel
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “You have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.” Secret on one side, broad daylight on the other. That's about as opposite as it gets. This is a heavy word, and I think David felt every bit of it.
Quiet and hidden is how David acted, not how the LORD answers. He says, “…I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.” Daylight, and all Israel watching. Nothing quiet about it.

Dark of night is where secrets like to live. But the LORD says, “…I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.” The secret was David's, and the daylight is the LORD's answer. Midnight is not on the schedule.

explanations.answer: I have sinned against the LORD
explanations.explanation: David says it plain: “I have sinned against the LORD.” No excuses, no long speech. Six words, and he owns it. I've made longer excuses over one burnt batch, so I respect that.

explanations.answer: I have done nothing in secret
explanations.explanation: David says the opposite. His words are, “I have sinned against the LORD.” The LORD had just told him, “You have acted in secret…” and David doesn't argue. He just owns it.

explanations.answer: I have kept the LORD's command
explanations.explanation: David doesn't claim any such thing. He says, “I have sinned against the LORD.” The LORD had asked why David despised His command, and David doesn't defend himself. I think that's the honest way to answer.

Nathan says the reverse: “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die.” Right after David owns his sin, those are the words he hears. The next verse says the son born to David will surely die, but David himself is told he will not. I think there's a lot of mercy packed in that one sentence.

Nathan tells him, “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die.” Taken away, and David lives. The consequence that follows is about the son born to him (2 Samuel 12:14), not David himself. The text puts mercy first.

explanations.answer: He pleads with God and fasts
explanations.explanation: The text says, “David pleaded with God for the boy.” He fasted too, and went into his house for the night. He took it straight to God. I think this is a hard stretch for David.

explanations.answer: He sends for Nathan to come back
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say David sent for Nathan, and Nathan had gone home (2 Samuel 12:15). What it does say is, “David pleaded with God for the boy.” David fasted too. He went straight to God with it.

explanations.answer: He goes out to join the battle
explanations.explanation: There's no battle in this part of the story. The text says David “…went into his house and spent the night lying in sackcloth on the ground.” Before that, “David pleaded with God for the boy.” The whole scene stays at home.

The text says the opposite. The elders of his household stood beside him to help him up from the ground, “…but he was unwilling and would not eat anything with them.” David stays right where he is. I think they only wanted to help.
David stays down. The elders of his household stood beside him to help him up, but he “…would not eat anything with them.” That's how the text puts it. I bet it was hard for them to watch.

They say, “…He may even harm himself.” They had spoken to David while the child was alive and he wouldn't listen, so they didn't know how he'd take the news. That's a heavy part of the story. I think they were afraid because they cared about him.
Their worry isn't about being punished. The only fear they name is, “…He may even harm himself.” It's about David himself, plain and simple. A heavy thing to say out loud.
Leaving the city isn't in their words at all. What they say is, “…He may even harm himself.” That's the only fear they name, and it's a serious one.

The text says, “When David saw that his servants were whispering to one another, he perceived that the child was dead.” He reads the room before anyone says a word. Hushed voices in a quiet house can say plenty. Then he asks them straight out.

explanations.answer: Nathan comes back to tell him
explanations.explanation: Nathan had gone home (2 Samuel 12:15), and the text never brings him back here. David works it out himself when he sees the whispering. Then he asks, “Is the child dead?”

explanations.answer: He hears mourners outside the house
explanations.explanation: No mourners are mentioned. The text says David saw his servants whispering to one another, and he perceived what had happened. Then he asked them, “Is the child dead?” They answered, “He is dead.”
Worships. David “…went into the house of the LORD and worshiped.” That comes before he asks for any food. Hard news, and the first place he goes is to the LORD.
Fasting is what David was doing while the child was alive. But the text says that in the house of the LORD he “worshiped.” That's where he goes first, before his own house.
Mourning is a fair guess for a hard day, and I think David was grieving. But the verse says he “…went into the house of the LORD and worshiped.” That's the word the text uses.
True. “Then he went to his own house, and at his request they set food before him, and he ate.” David asks, and they bring it. After the fast, I'd say that was a plain, quiet meal.
The text says it plainly: “Then he went to his own house, and at his request they set food before him, and he ate.” He asks, and they set it before him. That's what David does after worship.

explanations.answer: He hoped the LORD might let the child live
explanations.explanation: David gives his own reason: “…‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’” That's hope, resting on the LORD's grace. He fasted and wept because he hoped.

explanations.answer: Nathan had told him to do it
explanations.explanation: Nathan never tells him to fast in these verses. David gives his own reason: “…‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’” So it was hope, not an order.

explanations.answer: It was the custom for a king
explanations.explanation: Nobody here says it was a custom for a king. David gives the reason himself: “…‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’” That's a hope, not a habit.

David says the opposite: “But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.” While there was hope, he fasted. Now he asks what fasting could change.

David asks, “But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again?” He ends with, “I will go to him, but he will not return to me.” While the child was alive he fasted and wept, and now he lets that go. I think that's a hard thing to say out loud.

Solomon, David and Bathsheba's son. The text says, “…she gave birth to a son, and they named him Solomon.” It also says, “Now the LORD loved the child.” After a heavy chapter, that's a gentle note to land on.
Absalom was another of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:3), but he isn't the baby here. The text says, “…they named him Solomon.” Same dad, different boy.
Jonathan was David's close friend (1 Samuel 18:1), and he isn't the name here. The text says, “…they named him Solomon.” Good name, wrong baby.

The text gives the reason: the LORD “…sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him.” The name came with the LORD's love for the boy attached. After all the heavy parts, I think that line is the sweetest one in the chapter.
The text doesn't say Bathsheba asked. It says the LORD sent word through Nathan the prophet, and it gives the reason: “…because the LORD loved him.” The name comes from Him.
The servants don't show up in this part of the story at all. The LORD sent word through Nathan the prophet to name the boy Jedidiah. The reason is right there: “…because the LORD loved him.”
